sections.overview: The common eider is a heavy, sociable sea duck that rarely strays far from the coast. It is the heaviest duck in the United Kingdom and a strong, fast flier; its soft nest down gave the eiderdown its name.
sections.identification: An adult weighs about 2.1 kg in Britain, with a wing length near 29 cm; males are slightly larger. The breeding male is white above and black below, with a black cap and a pale green patch on each side of the head. The female is brown with dense dark barring, a camouflage that hides her on the nest. Young males need about three years to reach full adult plumage.
sections.habitat: It is a true sea duck, usually found close to shore in sandy bays or in long lines just beyond the breaking waves, and it is rarely seen on fresh water. It nests on rocky coasts and islands, often on small islands free of mammalian predators; in Britain and Ireland it breeds mainly around northern coasts and winters further south.
sections.diet: The eider feeds mostly on blue mussels and other molluscs, together with crustaceans and echinoderms such as crabs and sea urchins. It dives for them, in British waters typically to about 3 m, and swallows the shells whole before crushing them in its gizzard.
sections.behavior: Eiders are very sociable, riding the swell in groups and gathering in long lines offshore. In spring the males give loud, moaning courtship calls. Ducklings leave the nest soon after hatching and often join a crèche tended by several females, which lowers the risk for each individual chick.
sections.reproduction: In the UK there is usually one brood a year, with a clutch of typically four to six eggs. The female lines the nest with her own down and incubates alone for 25–28 days. The downy chicks feed themselves and fledge after about 65–75 days. Breeding typically starts at three years of age.
sections.ecology: By eating mussels and other shellfish, eiders shape the numbers of their prey, which has brought them into conflict with mussel farmers. Gulls are major predators of eggs and ducklings, and Arctic foxes take them where they can reach the nests, which is why islands without mammals are favoured. In Shetland, predation by marine mammals such as killer whales is one suspected factor in recent declines.
sections.conservation: The IUCN lists the common eider as Near Threatened. The UK breeding population was about 37,000 pairs in 2012–15, and the UK wintering population fell by 32% between 1998 and 2023. It is Amber-listed in the UK, partly because of its winter concentrations, which are vulnerable to oil spills and other pollution. The oldest ringed bird reached over 35 years.
